overview.text: The Hertzsprung–Russell (H–R) diagram is a graph astronomers use to compare stars by intrinsic brightness—usually luminosity or absolute magnitude—and surface temperature, often represented by spectral type or color. In the customary layout, hotter stars appear to the left and brighter stars higher up. Stars form recognizable groups rather than appearing randomly: the main sequence is a diagonal band running from hot, bright stars at the upper left to cool, faint stars at the lower right. Giants occupy a bright region above it, while white dwarfs are hot but faint and appear at the lower left. These patterns help astronomers study stars and their evolution.

key_facts.text: Ejnar Hertzsprung and Henry Norris Russell independently developed the diagram through studies in the early 1900s.
The horizontal axis can show surface temperature or spectral class; the vertical axis shows luminosity. Observational versions may instead use color and absolute magnitude.
The main sequence runs diagonally from hot, luminous stars to cool, faint stars; stars on it generate energy by fusing hydrogen into helium.
Giants are bright despite relatively cool surfaces and therefore appear above the main sequence; white dwarfs are hot but faint and appear at the lower left.
A star’s position reflects its properties and can help astronomers investigate its stage of evolution.
